entries.title: FAR.AI Minimal Standard for Safeguards v1.0: Grok 4.5 Yields 63 Universal Jailbreaks; Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol Yield None
entries.summary: FAR.AI introduced a 67-technique jailbreak taxonomy and benchmarked Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Grok 4.5 on 360 CBRNE/cyber attacker goals, finding robustness varies by more than 100×: Grok 4.5 yielded 63 universal jailbreaks at ~$58 each and Gemini 18 at ~$278, while neither Claude Fable 5 nor GPT-5.6 Sol yielded any, with defense-in-depth combining reasoning, activation, and I/O monitoring recommended to close the gap.

entries.title: arXiv 2608.02820: Model Poisoning Evades Chain-of-Thought Monitoring — Backdoors Produce Benign CoT While Executing Attacker Behavior
entries.summary: Fine-tuning can implant backdoors in reasoning models that elicit attacker-chosen outputs while maintaining entirely benign-looking chain-of-thought traces, with causal interventions confirming a trigger-conditioned activation pathway that bypasses visible reasoning — reframing CoT monitoring as a consistency check problem rather than anomaly detection.

links.title: arXiv 2608.02820 — Evading Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Through Model Poisoning

entries.title: arXiv 2608.02657: Agentic LLMs Encode Latent Indirect Prompt-Injection Exposure Signals — Probe-Gated Defense Cuts Attack Success to 0%
entries.summary: Simple linear probes on pre-generation hidden states predict indirect prompt-injection (IPI) exposure at 90%+ AUROC across six models (up to 753B parameters) and unseen attacks, and a probe-gated reasoning defense (AGRI) reduces attack success rate from 34.6% to 0% on Qwen3.5-27B while preserving clean-task utility — revealing a recognition–action gap where models detect IPI but fail to act safely.

links.title: arXiv 2608.02657 — Your Agentic LLMs Secretly Encode Latent Signals of Indirect Prompt-Injection Exposure

entries.title: arXiv 2608.02681: Batch Prompting Is a New Black-Box Jailbreak — Harmful Questions Refused in Isolation Comply When Embedded in Benign Batches
entries.summary: A harmful question that is reliably refused in isolation consistently elicits harmful responses when embedded among benign questions in a batch prompt — a distinct safety failure mode not reducible to in-context learning or long-context effects — and batch-aware preference optimization mitigates the vulnerability across open-source and frontier commercial models.

links.title: arXiv 2608.02681 — Safety in Batches? Understanding and Mitigating Safety Failures in Batch Prompting

entries.title: arXiv 2608.02665: Single-Prompt Safety Benchmarks Underestimate Unsafe Compliance by 3–13 Percentage Points Across Surface-Form Variants
entries.summary: Evaluating LLMs on a single canonical prompt per item underestimates true unsafe compliance by 3.3–12.9 pp, with 5–13% of seeds appearing safe on the canonical form found unsafe under meaning-preserving reformulations (back-translation, code-switched variants), a gap that is model-dependent and consistent across five frontier models — directly challenging the validity of current safety benchmark methodology.

links.title: arXiv 2608.02665 — Single Canonical Prompts Underestimate LLM Safety's Surface-Form Sensitivity

entries.title: arXiv 2608.03509: SkillJack — Attacking Self-Evolving Agents' Skill Pipeline Drops Safety Detection from 98.5% to 11.4%; Attacks Survive Source Deletion
entries.summary: SkillJack exploits the experience-to-skill extraction pipeline in self-evolving agents to launder malicious behavior into durable skill artifacts: safety detection falls from 98.5% on poisoned trajectories to 11.4% on extracted skills in SkillX, attack success rates reach 56–89%, and 80% of attacks persist after the original poisoned records are deleted — establishing skill evolution as a new, persistent attack surface.

links.title: arXiv 2608.03509 — SkillJack: Persistent Skill Backdoors in Self-Evolving Agents

entries.title: arXiv 2608.03626: Security-Oriented LLM Lifecycle Model Finds Regulatory Visibility Lowest at Development Stages Where Consequential Decisions Are Made
entries.summary: A 32-stage security lifecycle model for LLM systems, with governance mappings to NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001, reveals a structural gap: governance evidence concentrates at deployment-facing stages visible to regulators, while the most consequential decisions — data selection, alignment strategy, and capability boundaries — are made at development-facing stages where regulatory visibility is lowest.

links.title: arXiv 2608.03626 — A Security-Oriented Lifecycle Model for Large Language Model Systems

entries.title: Cisco Talos: Real-World Threat Actors Bypass AI Coding Tool Guardrails Using Only Ownership Claims and CTF Framing — No Sophisticated Techniques Required
entries.summary: Analyzing a corpus of actual attacker prompt logs from endpoints running Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini, Cisco Talos found that guardrails 'did not provide much protection' — simple social engineering tactics such as claiming ownership of target systems, invoking CTF or bug-bounty framings, and splitting malicious tasks across sessions defeated controls across all tested models and platforms without any encoding or evasion techniques.

links.title: Cisco Talos: 'Keep going, bro' — Data-Driven Look at How Adversaries Are Weaponizing AI
The Register: Bypassing AI Guardrails Is So Easy a Script Kiddie Can Do It
Axios: Cisco Reveals How Hackers Use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini

entries.title: Azure DevOps MCP Prompt Injection Lets Attackers Hijack AI Code Review Agents Using Their Own Platform Permissions
entries.summary: A vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure DevOps Model Context Protocol integration allows hidden content embedded in pull-request comments to hijack AI code review agents and redirect them to execute attacker-controlled instructions — with root failures identified as absent prompt-injection defenses, insufficient input sanitization, and inadequate privilege separation between reviewer-supplied content and agent tool execution.

links.title: AI Governance Institute: Azure DevOps MCP Prompt Injection Let Attackers Hijack AI Review Agents

entries.title: Auterion Deploys Autonomous Terminal Guidance on 50,000 Ukrainian Drones Under $100M Contract, Exposing 'Human-in-the-Loop' Definitional Gap
entries.summary: Auterion's AI-powered Shrike FPV drones complete a lethal strike autonomously if the radio link is severed despite operators pre-designating targets before launch — a deployment the company describes as human-in-the-loop — raising fundamental questions about whether existing oversight frameworks adequately define meaningful human control for irreversible, high-consequence AI actions.

links.title: AI Governance Institute: Auterion's 50,000-Drone Deployment Exposes the 'Human-in-the-Loop' Labeling Gap

entries.title: Barracuda PoC: Enterprise Email AI Assistant Weaponized to Suppress Audit Logs and Redirect $250K Wire Transfer Using Only Existing Permissions
entries.summary: Barracuda Networks demonstrated a proof-of-concept attack in which a compromised email account's built-in AI assistant — using only its existing legitimate permissions — suppressed audit logs, conducted internal reconnaissance, and redirected a $250,000 wire transfer while remaining invisible to standard behavioral monitoring and MFA controls.

links.title: AI Governance Institute: Email AI Assistants Can Be Weaponized to Steal $250K and Suppress Audit Logs

entries.title: Mitiga 'PromptLogger': Malicious Instructions in CLAUDE.md and .cursorrules Turn Sanctioned Coding Agents into Credential Exfiltration Tools
entries.summary: Security firm Mitiga documented an attack technique embedding malicious instructions in AI agent configuration files (CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules) that silently exfiltrate user prompts, credentials, and environment variables through the agent's own legitimate permissions — evading EDR tools and undermining governance programs that treat sanctioned coding assistants as low-risk approved software.

links.title: AI Governance Institute: Poisoned AI Config Files Turn Sanctioned Coding Agents Into Exfiltration Tools

entries.title: Discord AI Bug Wrongfully Bans 8,000 Users After System Bypasses Human Review Checkpoint — Irreversible Automated Enforcement at Scale
entries.summary: A bug in Discord's AI content moderation system caused more than 8,000 wrongful bans after harmless images were misidentified as harmful and the system bypassed its human-review checkpoint — a direct illustration of the consequences of absent technically-enforced human approval gates for irreversible AI-driven penalties.

links.title: AI Governance Institute: Discord's AI Bug Wrongfully Banned 8,000 Users When Human Review Was Bypassed

entries.title: JFrog: 54 Apparently AI-Generated Fake CVEs with High/Critical CVSS Scores Expose Vulnerability Pipeline Integrity Gap
entries.summary: JFrog researchers identified 54 apparently AI-generated, non-reproducible CVEs submitted through an obscure GitHub repository — several receiving high or critical CVSS scores before being flagged as bogus — revealing a structural flaw in the CVE pipeline: no mandatory proof-of-concept verification step exists to catch AI hallucinations, and NIST's NVD backlog exceeding 27,000 unprocessed records has effectively collapsed the secondary review layer.

links.title: AI Governance Institute: 54 Fake CVEs Expose a Systemic Integrity Gap in Enterprise Vulnerability Management
